ruled_out.assertion: JwtMiddleware is registered for the literal path 'invoices', so it never runs for /invoices/:id, /invoices/search, PATCH or DELETE, leaving them unauthenticated.
ruled_out.killed_by: billing-portal/src/app.module.ts:32 — the route is registered with method: RequestMethod.ALL. Nest's ExpressAdapter.createMiddlewareFactory returns app.use for RequestMethod.ALL, and Express's use() is prefix-matching, so /api/v1/invoices/<anything> is covered. Nest's RouteInfoPathExtractor also prepends the global prefix to middleware routes, so the 'api/v1' prefix from main.ts:23 does not orphan them either. Both sub-path coverage and prefix alignment hold.

The branch is unreachable over HTTP as the module is wired today. It is recorded here rather than deleted because it is one route registration away from being reachable.

ruled_out.assertion: authenticate() never reads the JWT header's alg, so an alg:none or algorithm-confusion token is accepted.
ruled_out.killed_by: edge-links/src/auth.ts:29-41 — verifySignature imports the key as {name: 'HMAC', hash: 'SHA-256'} unconditionally and calls crypto.subtle.verify with it. Ignoring the header is what makes this safe, not unsafe.

findings.title: Free-text invoice memo search interpolates the query parameter into raw SQL
findings.evidence: db.raw builds `and memo ilike '%${term}%'` by template interpolation while the tenant on line 54 is bound with a `?` placeholder — the two values in the same statement are handled differently. `term` is the `q` query parameter, taken raw at invoices.controller.ts:61 (`@Query('q') q = ''`) and handed to searchByMemo at line 62 with no transformation. It is a primitive query parameter, so the global ValidationPipe (main.ts:25, whitelist/transform) does not constrain it: whitelist strips unknown properties of DTO classes and there is no DTO here. A single quote in `q` terminates the literal inside the raw string.
findings.impact: Any authenticated portal user can append arbitrary SQL to a statement that runs with the application's Postgres role — reading every tenant's invoices, customer ids and amounts through UNION or a boolean oracle, and reaching any other table the role can see. The bound tenant_id parameter does not constrain the injected clause.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: `where memo ilike ?` with `[tenantId, '%' + term + '%']`, or use knex's `.whereILike('memo', `%${term}%`)` builder, which parameterises. Never mix a bound parameter and an interpolated one in the same raw string.

triage.reason: There is no allowlist, cast or escaping between the controller and the sink. The one binding on the path (line 54) covers tenant_id only; the interpolation on line 51 is outside the bindings array entirely.
The value originates at invoices.controller.ts:61 as `@Query('q')`, i.e. the raw request query string, and reaches line 51 through a single unmodified function argument.
The sink is knex's db.raw, which sends the assembled string to Postgres for parsing. The comment on lines 34-37 claiming knex quotes the identifier applies to orderBy on line 40, not to this string.

findings.title: Invoice detail cache is keyed by invoice id alone, so the tenant filter is short-circuited
findings.evidence: The cache key is `invoice:${invoiceId}` while the loader closure `() => this.repo.findForTenant(tenantId, invoiceId)` is the only place the tenant appears. TtlCache (common/cache.ts:17-24) returns the stored value on any key hit within 30s without re-running the loader, so the `where({tenant_id, id})` at invoice.repository.ts:30 never executes for the second caller. The cache instance is a field of the singleton InvoicesService (line 23), so it is shared by every request in the process, and the class comment on common/cache.ts:7-9 confirms one process serves the region. Both files are individually correct: findForTenant scopes properly, and TtlCache memoises exactly what it is asked to.
findings.impact: Tenant B requesting GET /api/v1/invoices/<id> within 30 seconds of tenant A reading the same id receives tenant A's invoice row — customer id, amount and status — even though tenantFor() and findForTenant() both did their jobs. Invalidation at line 55 is keyed the same way, so a status change by one tenant also clears another's entry.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant in the key: `invoice:${tenantId}:${invoiceId}`. More durably, make the cache API refuse a key that does not carry the scope its loader closes over, so the omission cannot recur silently.

triage.reason: The only tenant control on this path is inside the loader, and the cache hit at common/cache.ts:18-20 returns before the loader is called. No mandatory layer sits between the controller and the cache: tenantFor() at invoices.controller.ts:67 resolves the caller's own tenant correctly and then that value is discarded by the key.
TtlCache is constructed unconditionally at invoices.service.ts:23 and used on the default GET :id route; no flag or environment gates it.
The boundary is the tenant. jwt.middleware.ts:40 establishes tenantId per session and invoice.repository.ts:30 treats it as a filter, which is the definition of a second principal.
The cached value is an InvoiceRow: customer_id, amount_cents, status and memo for a named customer of another tenant.

findings.title: The staff-only guard tests a path prefix that the global route prefix makes unreachable
findings.evidence: STAFF_PREFIXES holds '/admin', '/internal' and '/ops' and isStaffPath tests `path.startsWith(prefix)` against `req.path` (line 22). main.ts:23 calls `app.setGlobalPrefix('api/v1')`, and Nest registers controller routes on the root Express app rather than on a mounted sub-router, so Express's req.path getter returns the full pathname — `/api/v1/admin/reports`, which starts with '/api', not '/admin'. isStaffPath therefore returns false for every request the application serves, canActivate takes the early return on line 26, and the `user.staff !== true` check on line 30 is never reached. Two files, each correct on its own: the prefix list is a sensible list, and the global prefix is a deliberate deployment choice.
findings.impact: The one control asserting that /admin traffic belongs to internal staff never fires. Combined with the missing @Roles on AdminReportsController's PATCH and DELETE (reported separately), any authenticated tenant customer reaches the reporting surface. The guard reads as present in review, which is why the gap survives.
findings.recommendation: Compare against the prefixed path — build the list from the same constant used in setGlobalPrefix, or match on `context.getClass()` metadata rather than on a string. Add a startup assertion that at least one registered route matches each entry in STAFF_PREFIXES, so a prefix change fails the build instead of silently disabling the guard.

triage.reason: RolesGuard (the other APP_GUARD, app.module.ts:24) returns true whenever a handler carries no @Roles metadata (roles.guard.ts:25-27), and AdminReportsController's @Patch(':id') and @Delete(':id') carry none. Nothing else asserts `staff`.
This is a control that cannot fire, not a tainted value reaching a sink.

There is no reading on which req.path omits the global prefix. Express defines req.path as parseurl(req).pathname, and setGlobalPrefix does not rewrite req.url; the fallback `req.originalUrl` on line 22 would carry the prefix too, and is unreachable because req.path is always defined.

findings.title: Admin report update and delete carry no role requirement while their sibling create does
findings.evidence: In one controller class: @Post() createDefinition (line 90) and @Post('reconciliation') reconcile (line 107) both carry @Roles('billing_ops'); @Get() listDefinitions (line 85), @Patch(':id') updateDefinition (line 96) and @Delete(':id') deleteDefinition (line 101) carry nothing. RolesGuard returns true when the metadata is absent (roles.guard.ts:25-27), and AdminScopeGuard is inert for the reason given in the previous finding, so the mutating verbs are gated by authentication alone. The asymmetry is decidable inside this file: three handlers reach report definitions, one is gated and two are not.
findings.impact: Any authenticated portal user — any tenant's customer, with no billing role at all — can modify or delete report definitions belonging to the operator's reporting surface. GET additionally leaks the definitions list scoped by tenantFor(req).
findings.recommendation: Apply @Roles('billing_ops') at the class level on AdminReportsController and let individual handlers narrow rather than widen, so a new handler inherits the gate instead of defaulting open.

triage.reason: The only layer that could compensate is AdminScopeGuard, and admin-scope.guard.ts:15 never matches the served path. No base class, interceptor or service-layer check exists — the handler bodies at lines 97-98 and 102-103 are the whole implementation.
No external gateway is claimed anywhere in this repository for the admin surface; the comment at app.module.ts:29-30 places the reporting surface under the same middleware as ordinary tenant traffic.
The three handlers reach the same resource family (report definitions keyed by the same :id) — they differ only in verb, which is precisely the asymmetry WEB-24 names.

findings.title: Reconciliation bulk upsert writes invoices with no tenant scope and no status-transition check
findings.evidence: The `invoices` table has two writers. updateStatus (line 58) scopes with `where({tenant_id, id})` and is only reachable through changeStatus (invoices.service.ts:47-57), which loads the row for the caller's tenant and enforces ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS — a table whose comment on lines 10-13 says a paid invoice may never be reopened. bulkUpsert does neither: it takes `rows` straight from `body.rows ?? []` (invoices.controller.ts:110) through importReconciled (invoices.service.ts:67-69), casts `Partial<InvoiceRow>[]` to `InvoiceRow[]`, and runs `.onConflict('id').merge(['status','amount_cents','memo','updated_at'])`. tenant_id is never stamped and never compared, and the merge is keyed on the client-supplied `id` alone. `@Body() body: any` (controller line 109) means the whitelist ValidationPipe at main.ts:25 has no DTO to enforce.
findings.impact: A caller holding billing_ops can rewrite the status, amount and memo of any invoice in any tenant by naming its id in the rows array — including flipping a `paid` invoice back to `open` or `draft`, which the transition table exists to prevent and which the comment says the general ledger export depends on. Rows with unseen ids are inserted outright.
findings.recommendation: Give the endpoint a DTO with a declared field allowlist, stamp tenant_id from the session on every row, and route the write through the same transition check changeStatus uses — or add `where tenant_id = ?` to the merge and reject any row whose current status has no transition to the incoming one.

triage.reason: @Roles('billing_ops') on invoices.controller.ts:108 is an authentication-level gate on who may call the endpoint; it asserts nothing about which tenant's rows the body may name, and nothing re-checks the transition table. The path from controller to knex passes through no validator.
The two writers reach the same effect on the same table: both set `status`, `amount_cents` and `updated_at` on a row of `invoices`. The difference is not the destination, it is the checks.

The comment at invoices.service.ts:63-66 says the bank matcher has already resolved every line, but the endpoint is an ordinary HTTP POST reachable by any billing_ops holder, not a private feed with its own authentication.

findings.title: Authentication returns a full-scope session whenever ENVIRONMENT is not the exact string "production", and the production deployment sets "prod"
findings.evidence: authenticate() returns `{sub: 'dashboard', owner: 'dashboard', role: 'owner', scopes: SCOPES_ALL}` before reading any header when `env.ENVIRONMENT !== "production"`. wrangler.toml never produces that string: [vars] sets "dev" (line 7), [env.staging] sets "staging" (line 36) and [env.production] sets ENVIRONMENT = "prod" (line 40). A grep for "production" across edge-links returns only auth.ts:50. SCOPES_ALL is ROLE_SCOPES.owner (roles.ts:8), i.e. links:read, links:write, links:delete and links:admin. Two files each defensible on their own: a shortcut for non-production, and a deployment that spells its environment "prod".
findings.impact: Every request to the production Worker is authenticated as the owner of a workspace named "dashboard" with no credential presented. index.ts:99 derives the Durable Object id from session.owner, so an anonymous caller reads, writes and deletes that workspace's links, and reaches the /do/* passthrough and /api/preview with owner scopes.
findings.recommendation: Invert the test — treat any environment that is not explicitly a known development one as production and require a token — and add a boot assertion that ENVIRONMENT is one of an enumerated set so an unrecognised value fails closed rather than opening the door.

triage.reason: The early return on line 51 precedes the Authorization header read on line 54, so no signature check, expiry check or key check runs. index.ts:94-97 accepts whatever authenticate returns.
The branch is not gated by a build flag or a dev-only file: it is the shipped src/auth.ts, selected at runtime by a [vars] value that wrangler.toml sets to "prod" for the production deployment.

The comment on lines 48-49 claims a team Access policy for preview and staging only. This finding is scoped to the production deployment — the one whose [env.production] ENVIRONMENT value of "prod" trips the branch — and no external control is claimed for it anywhere in the repository. FP-08 asks whether a claimed out-of-repo control exculpates; there is no such claim covering the affected environment, so the rule does not reach this finding rather than being unresolvable. If the intent had been to cover production too, the answer would be UNKNOWN and this would ship as probable.

findings.title: A token with no role claim resolves to the owner scope set, not to the viewer set the same function falls back to
findings.evidence: `export function scopesFor(role: string = "owner")` — the default parameter is the owner role, while the body's fallback for an *unrecognised* role string is `ROLE_SCOPES.viewer` (line 15). The two disagree: an unknown role is treated conservatively, a missing one is treated as owner. A missing role is reachable: index.ts:49-59 reads `ws-meta:<workspace>` from KV and puts `role: meta?.role` into the payload, so when the KV entry is absent or carries no role, JSON.stringify omits the key entirely; auth.ts:75-76 then calls scopesFor(claims.role) with undefined, the default fires, and the session receives links:read, links:write, links:delete and links:admin. hasScope (line 19) treats links:admin as satisfying every scope. The comment on lines 10-13 states outright that pre-migration workspaces have no role, so the case is expected rather than hypothetical.
findings.impact: Any workspace whose ws-meta entry is missing or roleless mints tokens with full administrative scope. A viewer-intent workspace silently gets write, delete and admin over its links; createLink's hasScope check (links.ts:61) and the Durable Object's three scope tests (LinkStore.ts:38,47,55) all pass.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default and make the parameter required (`scopesFor(role: string | undefined)`) with an explicit `if (!role) return ROLE_SCOPES.viewer;` so the missing case lands where the unknown case already lands. Refuse to mint a token when ws-meta carries no role, rather than emitting one without the claim.

triage.reason: No layer re-derives the role. auth.ts:76 stores scopesFor's return on the session, index.ts:118 forwards it verbatim to the Durable Object, and links.ts:60 recomputes it from the same undefined role. Nothing consults KV again at request time.

The absence of the claim is producible by an attacker only indirectly, but it does not need to be attacker-produced: it is the documented state of every pre-migration workspace, and possession of that workspace's secret is the only precondition.

The benign reading — 'the ?? on line 15 protects it' — is exactly wrong: `??` only fires when the lookup misses, and the default parameter has already replaced undefined with "owner" before the lookup runs, so ROLE_SCOPES["owner"] hits and the fallback never applies. default_resolver.py flagged line 15 and line 19 (the two `??`/`||` fallbacks) and did not name line 14; the tool pointed at the right file and the wrong line, and the finding is the default parameter.

findings.title: The /do/* passthrough forwards the client's X-Actor-Scopes header to the Durable Object that trusts it
findings.evidence: `new Request(url, request)` copies the incoming request's method, body and headers onto the rewritten URL, and the result is handed to `stub.fetch(forwarded)` unmodified. LinkStore.actorScopes (do/LinkStore.ts:14-19) derives the caller's capabilities entirely from the X-Actor-Scopes header, and its own comment on line 13 states the assumption this branch violates: 'Scopes are stamped on by the router once it has authenticated the caller.' Every other caller honours that: createLink sets the header from scopesFor(session.role) (handlers/links.ts:76), and the list branch sets it from session.scopes (index.ts:118). The /do/* branch sets nothing and strips nothing. The DO's switch (line 25) exposes /put, /list and /delete, all reachable as /do/put, /do/list and /do/delete.
findings.impact: A session holding only `links:read` (a viewer) sends `X-Actor-Scopes: links:admin` to POST /do/put or /do/delete and passes all three scope tests inside the Durable Object, gaining write and delete over the workspace's links. The role system is defeated for any caller who reads it. The object id is still derived from session.owner (line 99), so this escalates within a workspace rather than across workspaces — but with the previous finding live in production, that session is anonymous.
findings.recommendation: Delete the header from the forwarded request and set it from the session, exactly as the two sibling branches do: build the Request, then `forwarded.headers.set('X-Actor-Scopes', session.scopes.join(','))`. Better, stop passing raw client requests through and expose only the specific DO operations the dashboard needs.

triage.reason: The only control between the client and the DO is authenticate() at index.ts:94, which establishes identity and then does nothing about this header. No middleware strips inbound X-Actor-Scopes anywhere in the Worker.
X-Actor-Scopes is an ordinary request header on a request the client composes; nothing in the Cloudflare runtime reserves or rewrites it, unlike CF-Connecting-IP.
The second principal is the workspace role boundary — viewer, editor and owner are distinct principals in ROLE_SCOPES, and the Durable Object enforces exactly that boundary on lines 38, 47 and 55.

findings.title: Unauthenticated open redirect through the /go/ inline destination parameter
findings.evidence: `const inline = url.searchParams.get("to"); if (inline) { return Response.redirect(inline, 302); }` — the value goes to the redirect with no parse, no scheme test and no host allowlist, and it is checked before the KV slug lookup so no stored link is needed. index.ts:90-92 dispatches /go/ before the authenticate() call on line 94, so the branch takes no credential. The contrast is visible one function down: preview() at line 47 does apply a scheme test and an exact-host allowlist to its own URL parameter.
findings.impact: https://<link-host>/go/x?to=https://attacker.example redirects a visitor off the organisation's shortener domain while carrying its reputation, which is the standard phishing primitive for a link service. The redirect is unauthenticated, uncacheable to a fixed target, and indistinguishable in the URL bar from a legitimate short link.
findings.recommendation: Parse with `new URL(inline)`, require an https scheme, and either restrict the host to an allowlist or drop the inline path and require the campaign builder to persist a slug like every other destination.

triage.reason: No allowlist is consulted on this branch. ALLOWED_PREVIEW_HOSTS (line 11) is referenced only by preview() at line 47; the redirect path never reads it.
The value is url.searchParams.get('to') from the request line, reaching Response.redirect in the next statement.

A link shortener redirecting to arbitrary destinations by design would redirect to *stored* destinations an authenticated workspace member chose. This branch accepts a destination from whoever composes the URL, which is a different exposure from the one the service intends.

findings.title: javascript: destinations pass link validation and are written into an href attribute
findings.evidence: parseLinkInput validates the target only with `new URL(target)` inside a try/catch (lines 39-43), which accepts `javascript:alert(1)` as a well-formed URL, then applies escapeHtml (line 49). escapeHtml replaces `& < > " '` and touches no scheme, so `javascript:alert(document.cookie)` survives verbatim. render.ts:16 writes it as `<a class="link-card__target" href="${link.target}">`, an attribute-and-URL context where HTML entity escaping is not the applicable escaping. The pack names this case directly: `href="{{ url }}"` accepts `javascript:`.
findings.impact: A workspace member with links:write stores a link whose target is a javascript: URL; any member who opens the dashboard list at GET /api/links and clicks it executes script in the dashboard origin with that viewer's session. escapeHtml's presence makes the flaw read as handled during review.
findings.recommendation: Test the parsed scheme after `new URL(target)` and accept only http: and https:. Escaping is the wrong control for a URL context; an allowlist of schemes is the right one.

triage.reason: escapeHtml at links.ts:14-21 is the only transformation on the path and it does not constrain the scheme. render.ts:10-12 states the invariant it relies on — 'already escaped by the API layer' — which is true and insufficient for an href.
target is body.target from the JSON request body (line 35), constrained only by length (1-2048) and URL well-formedness.
The sink is an href attribute in a text/html response (render.ts:31), which browsers execute for the javascript: scheme on activation.
There is no CSP header on the response (render.ts:30-32 sets only content-type) that would reduce this to informational, and the payload runs in the dashboard origin.

findings.title: The queue import path writes links without the validation and escaping the API path applies
findings.evidence: Two writers reach the same `link:<slug>` storage key in LinkStore.put (do/LinkStore.ts:42). createLink runs parseLinkInput first, which enforces SLUG_RE, a 1-2048 length bound, URL well-formedness and escapeHtml on both target and title (handlers/links.ts:27-52). handleQueue sends `{slug: row.slug, target: row.target, title: row.title ?? row.slug, owner: row.owner}` (lines 32-37) — the message body verbatim, with no parse, no slug pattern and no escaping — and hardcodes `X-Actor-Scopes: links:write` (line 31) so the DO's own gate passes. render.ts's stated invariant on lines 10-12 ('Fields arrive from the store already escaped by the API layer') is true of one writer and false of the other; linkCard interpolates title into element content and target into an href with no escaping of its own. `owner` is also taken from the message, so a message chooses which workspace's Durable Object it writes to (line 23).
findings.impact: A title or target carrying markup — `` — reaches the dashboard list page unescaped and executes in the viewer's session. A message can also write into any workspace by naming its owner, and can bypass SLUG_RE to create keys the API would reject.
findings.recommendation: Call parseLinkInput(row, row.owner) inside handleQueue so both writers share one validator, and derive the owner from the message's authenticated producer rather than from the row.

triage.reason: Nothing between the queue message and this.state.storage.put validates or escapes: LinkStore.put (do/LinkStore.ts:37-44) checks only the scope header, which handleQueue supplies itself, and then stores the parsed JSON as given.

The two writers reach the same effect — a StoredLink under the same `link:` prefix in the same Durable Object, read back by the same list handler and rendered by the same linkCard. They differ only in what they check.

The producer is not in this tree: wrangler.toml:30-32 declares an IMPORTS binding but no code in edge-links produces to link-imports, and the comment on queue.ts:13-14 attributes the rows to a dashboard CSV importer. Whether an outside caller controls a row therefore cannot be established here, which caps this finding at probable. What would settle it: the importer that publishes to the link-imports queue and whether it validates the CSV. The asymmetry itself is confirmed regardless.

findings.title: The credential endpoint is outside the rate-limited prefixes, and the limiter it does apply cannot count
findings.evidence: LIMITED_PREFIXES is ['/api/', '/go/'] and isLimited tests startsWith, so POST /auth/token — the workspace-secret verification endpoint dispatched at index.ts:86 — is never metered; index.ts:82 skips consume() entirely for it. Separately, consume (lines 28-37) reads the counter with `env.LINKS.get(key)`, compares, then writes back with put: a read-modify-write across an eventually-consistent KV store with no atomic increment, so concurrent requests all read the same value and all write current+1. The comment at lines 5-8 names the two surfaces that get scraped and omits the one that verifies a secret.
findings.impact: Workspace secrets can be guessed at unlimited rate against /auth/token, and a success mints a one-hour token. On the prefixes that are metered, the 120-per-window budget is not enforced under concurrency and is per-edge-location besides, so the declared limit overstates what is applied.
findings.recommendation: Add '/auth/' to LIMITED_PREFIXES and key the credential bucket on the workspace name as well as the IP. Replace the KV counter with a Durable Object or the Workers rate-limiting binding, which increments atomically.

triage.reason: index.ts:82 is the only place consume() is called, and it is guarded by isLimited(url.pathname), which returns false for /auth/token. No other limiter exists in the Worker.

Cloudflare offers account-level WAF rate limiting that could cover /auth/token, but no such rule is present in wrangler.toml or anywhere in this repository. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS. The atomicity half of the finding is unaffected by it and is confirmed from ratelimit.ts:30-36 alone.
An intentionally unmetered surface would be one where repetition costs nothing; this one verifies a shared secret with constantTimeEquals (index.ts:44) and issues a bearer token on success.

findings.title: Attestation verification computes a digest it never compares and returns a value that is always true
findings.evidence: The final statement is `digest.isNotEmpty()`, where digest is `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(...)` — SHA-256 always returns 32 bytes, so the expression is a tautology and the function has no path that returns false on the signature. The three earlier tests are: nonce equality against a nonce the server hands to anyone (Devices.kt:80-83 issues one for any serial with no scope check), `certificateChainSha256` equality against config.attestationRootFingerprint — a value published in plaintext at application.conf:27 — and `blob.signature.length < 64`, a length test on an attacker-chosen string. No key, no public key of the device, no chain parse, no comparison of the computed digest to anything. The docstring on lines 60-63 states what it claims to confirm: that the request 'was produced by a board holding a key signed by the manufacturing root'.
findings.impact: Any caller with a valid fleet-jwt can enroll an arbitrary serial with an attacker-chosen publicKey: GET /api/devices/<serial>/nonce for the nonce, copy the fingerprint out of application.conf, send any 64-character signature. Neither /nonce nor POST /api/devices/enroll calls requireScope at all (Devices.kt:80, 85), unlike their siblings on lines 76 and 108, so the lowest-privilege token in the fleet suffices. The device identity that everything downstream trusts is forgeable.
findings.recommendation: Verify the signature: parse the certificate chain, check it against the pinned root, and verify blob.signature over the computed digest with the leaf's public key, returning false on every failure. Add a negative test that a valid-looking blob with a wrong signature is rejected — the current implementation cannot fail such a test. Add requireScope to /enroll and /nonce.

triage.reason: Attestation.verify is the whole control on the enrolment path: Devices.kt:89-101 branches on its result and enrolls on true. No mTLS layer compensates — requireMutualTls (Config.kt:26) has no readers anywhere in the module, reported separately.
This is the shipped implementation called from the production enrolment route; no flag, test double or environment switch selects it.

There is no reading on which `digest.isNotEmpty()` can be false — MessageDigest.digest never returns an empty array for SHA-256. The three preceding tests are real branches, which is what makes the function read as a verifier.
This is not defence in depth that happens to be absent: it is the load-bearing control, and the project believes it holds it.

findings.title: An enrolment rejected for failed attestation is parked and replayed by a route that checks no attestation
findings.evidence: DeviceRegistry.stashPending has exactly one caller, and it is inside the failure arm: Devices.kt:94-100 runs `if (!attested) { DeviceRegistry.stashPending(request); respond(Forbidden) }`. By construction the `pending` map contains only enrolments that failed attestation. Enrollment.kt:50-57 then reads that map and calls `DeviceRegistry.enroll(parked.serial, parked.model, parked.publicKey)` with no attestation call of any kind, responding with the created device. The comment on lines 42-45 states the premise that makes it look safe — 'The stored request is the one the device already sent, so it goes straight to the registry' — which is true and is precisely the problem: the request it already sent is the one that was rejected.
findings.impact: Attestation is bypassable in two steps by anyone holding devices:write (which, per the next finding, is any service token): POST /api/devices/enroll with a deliberately invalid attestation to park the request, then POST /api/enrollment/<serial>/retry to have it enrolled. This defeats the enrolment gate even if Attestation.verify were implemented correctly, so it is an independent defect rather than a consequence of the previous one.
findings.recommendation: Do not park a request that failed verification — park only requests that failed for an infrastructure reason, and record why. On retry, re-run Attestation.verify against a freshly issued nonce before calling enroll.

triage.reason: The only gate on the retry route is requireScope("devices:write") at Enrollment.kt:47, which authorises the operator and asserts nothing about the device. DeviceRegistry.enroll (Devices.kt:51-57) performs no verification of its own.

The benign reading would be that `pending` also holds requests parked for transient reasons. It does not: grep for stashPending returns one call site, in the `!attested` branch, so the map's entire population is rejected enrolments.
Both routes are registered unconditionally inside the authenticated block at Application.kt:64-68.

findings.title: requireScope accepts any service token for any scope by default, and only one of five call sites opts out
findings.evidence: `allowServiceToken: Boolean = true` means a call site that says nothing grants every scope to any subject beginning with `svc-` (isServiceToken, line 17): lines 34-37 return true before the `scope` claim is ever read on line 42. The call sites are Devices.kt:76 (devices:read), Devices.kt:108 (devices:write, `allowServiceToken = false` — the only opt-out), Enrollment.kt:28 and :47 (devices:write), Firmware.kt:41 and :61 (firmware:read) and Firmware.kt:47 (firmware:publish). Six of seven omit the argument. The docstring on lines 12-16 asserts the compensating control — 'The JWT verifier already pins the audience they are issued for' — but audience is a property of the whole API (fleet-api, application.conf:18), identical for the operator console and the build pipeline, so it separates nothing.
findings.impact: A machine token issued for the narrowest purpose reaches firmware:publish, which moves a release channel onto a new build for every device in the fleet, and devices:write on the bulk enrolment route. The scope claim is decorative for the entire service surface except decommission. That the one security-relevant opt-out exists on line 108 shows the parameter was understood and then omitted six times.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default to `allowServiceToken: Boolean = false` so a route that wants machine access says so, and check the scope claim for service tokens too rather than short-circuiting on the subject prefix.

triage.reason: The JWT plugin at Application.kt:44-56 validates issuer, audience and a non-blank subject; it asserts nothing about scope. No route-level interceptor sits between authenticate("fleet-jwt") and the handler bodies.
No external policy is claimed for scope enforcement; the docstring points at the JWT verifier inside this repository, which application.conf:18 shows issues one audience for the whole API.

The comment on lines 14-16 frames the prefix as choosing 'the right audit label rather than a trust decision on its own', but lines 34-37 make it exactly a trust decision: it returns true and the scope check below is skipped.

findings.title: The /internal routes are registered outside the authentication block and reach the same effects as scoped routes
findings.evidence: Application.kt:58-73 places deviceRoutes, enrollmentRoutes and firmwareRoutes inside `rateLimit { authenticate("fleet-jwt") { ... } }` and calls internalRoutes(config) outside both, on the same Netty listener (one port, application.conf:3). None of the four handlers in Internal.kt calls requireScope or reads a principal. The asymmetry is exact: POST /internal/firmware/pin (line 52-56) calls FirmwareCatalog.publish — the identical writer that POST /api/firmware/publish reaches — while that sibling requires firmware:publish and validates `release.sha256.length != 64` (Firmware.kt:47-53). /internal/devices dumps DeviceRegistry.all(), the same body GET /api/devices returns behind devices:read. /internal/devices/rotate-key returns a freshly generated 32-byte provisioning key for any known serial.
findings.impact: Firmware channels can be repointed at an arbitrary artifact with an arbitrary or malformed checksum, the device inventory read, and provisioning keys minted, all with no credential. Repointing a channel is the highest-value operation in the service: every device pulling that channel follows it.
findings.recommendation: Move internalRoutes inside the authenticate block and add requireScope on each handler with the same scope its /api sibling requires — firmware:publish for pin, devices:read for the listing, a dedicated scope for rotate-key — and apply the same sha256 validation. Network placement can then remain a second layer rather than the only one.

triage.reason: No in-process control covers these routes: they are outside the authenticate block at Application.kt:64, they call no requireScope, and Ktor installs no global authorization plugin. FirmwareCatalog.publish (Firmware.kt:29-31) performs no checks of its own.

The routes serve on the same listener and port as the public API (application.conf:2-5); there is no separate binding, no localhost-only address and no second engine connector that would put them in one trust domain with the caller.

The comment on Internal.kt:28-31 claims 'These endpoints are only routed from inside the cluster network by the fleet control plane.' No ingress rule, NetworkPolicy, service mesh config or proxy configuration is present anywhere in fleet-provision to evidence that, and per FP-08 an unevidenced external control is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. This is what caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the ingress or mesh policy for this service. Note that even if it held, the finding moves rather than disappearing — an operator inside the mesh still reaches firmware publication without firmware:publish.
The /internal prefix is a naming convention, not a binding; Ktor routes it from the same listener as /api.

findings.title: Firmware artifact download builds a filesystem path from an unvalidated path parameter
findings.evidence: `val name = call.parameters["name"].orEmpty(); val artifact = File(config.firmwareDir, name)` — the value goes from the route parameter into a two-argument File constructor with no canonicalisation, no basename, no character allowlist and no containment test against firmwareDir, and is then streamed with call.respondFile (line 69) after only an isFile test. The contrast is instructive: helpdesk-live faces the same problem at attachment_controller.ex:50-53 and solves it with Path.basename plus an anchored pattern, so the shape of the missing control is not exotic.
findings.impact: A caller holding firmware:read (or any service token, per the requireScope finding) reads arbitrary files the service process can open — /etc/passwd, the JVM's environment, adjacent secrets under /var/lib — as long as the traversal survives into `name`.
findings.recommendation: Reduce to a basename and match an anchored allowlist pattern, then canonicalise and assert the resolved path is inside firmwareDir before opening: `File(firmwareDir, name).canonicalFile.startsWith(File(firmwareDir).canonicalFile)`.

triage.reason: There is no canonicalisation or containment check anywhere on the path; the only test is `artifact.isFile` on line 65, which a traversed path satisfies.
The value is call.parameters["name"], taken from the request URI.

Exploitability turns on framework behaviour I cannot establish from this tree: a single Ktor `{name}` placeholder matches one path segment, so a literal `/` cannot appear in it, and the attack needs a percent-encoded separator (`..%2f..%2f`) to survive segmentation and then be decoded into the parameter value. I believe Ktor 2.3.10 splits the raw path into segments and percent-decodes each segment afterwards, which would make it work, but I have not read that source and will not assert it. Per the triage rules an UNKNOWN caps this at probable. What would settle it: a single unit test issuing GET /api/firmware/artifact/..%2f..%2fetc%2fhostname against a test host and asserting the resolved path stays inside firmwareDir. The missing containment check is confirmed regardless of how the encoding resolves.

findings.title: The token endpoint lets the client choose its own scope and signs under the identity provider's issuer with a local symmetric secret
findings.evidence: Two defects in one handler. First, `val scope = form["scope"] ?: "devices:read"` (line 38) is copied verbatim into the minted token by `.withClaim("scope", scope)` (line 56) — the client names its own authorisation and no per-client allowlist, registry or intersection is consulted. A holder of any client credentials can request `scope=firmware:publish devices:write`. Second, the token is stamped `.withIssuer(config.issuer)` and `.withAudience(config.audience)` — https://id.example.com/ and fleet-api (application.conf:17-18) — and signed with `Algorithm.HMAC256(config.signingSecret)` (line 59), while this service's own verifier is built from the corporate JWKS at that issuer (Application.kt:39-50), an EC P-256 key per the sample in application.conf:29-33. A JWKS-backed verifier will not accept an HS256 token, so the endpoint mints credentials its own API rejects, under an issuer it does not own.
findings.impact: Either reading is bad. If some relying party accepts HS256 for iss=https://id.example.com/, this endpoint is an issuer-spoofing oracle: anyone holding the shared FLEET_SIGNING_SECRET, or any client that can drive the endpoint, obtains a token indistinguishable from one the corporate IdP issued, with a scope of their choosing. If no party accepts it, the client-credentials grant is broken and the whole flow silently does not work.
findings.recommendation: Bind the grantable scopes to the client record and intersect the requested scope with them, rejecting anything outside. Sign with a key this service legitimately owns under an issuer it owns, or delete the endpoint and let clients go to the real IdP.

triage.reason: Nothing between form["scope"] on line 38 and withClaim on line 56 narrows the value; clientSecretHash (line 17) authenticates the client and returns a hash, carrying no scope information.
Both `scope` and `client_id` come from the posted form parameters (lines 36-38).

Which relying parties accept a token bearing iss=https://id.example.com/ and how they verify it is outside this repository. That is what caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the verifier configuration of any service consuming fleet-api tokens — specifically whether any of them accepts HS256 for that issuer. The scope self-selection half needs no external evidence and stands on Token.kt:38 and :56 alone.
tokenRoutes is registered unconditionally at Application.kt:61, deliberately ahead of the authenticated surface.

findings.title: requireMutualTls is never read, and its predicate cannot match the environment the configuration sets
findings.evidence: Two independent reasons the control does not exist. It has zero readers: grep across fleet-provision returns only the declaration on lines 25-26 — Application.kt installs ContentNegotiation, CallLogging, RateLimit and Authentication and never consults it, and no engine connector, keystore or trustStore appears in application.conf. And its predicate is `environment == "prod"` while application.conf:13 sets `environment = "production"` and the vocabulary comment on line 12 enumerates 'dev, staging, production' — "prod" is not a value this configuration can hold. The docstring on lines 21-24 states the control it stands for: 'Devices present a manufacturing certificate on the TLS handshake... the service terminates TLS itself, so it is the one that has to demand the client certificate.' Compare debugRoutesEnabled on line 30, whose "dev" does appear in that vocabulary and which has a real reader at Devices.kt:117.
findings.impact: The device-certificate requirement that the code documents and that operators would read as present is not applied anywhere. It is also the layer that would have compensated for the enrolment attestation being inert, so its absence is what makes that finding reachable by any authenticated caller rather than by a caller holding a manufacturing certificate.
findings.recommendation: Either implement it — configure the Netty connector's SSL context with a trust manager and require the client certificate when the flag is set — or delete the property so nothing reads as a control that is not one. Whichever, align the string with the documented vocabulary and assert at boot that fleet.environment is one of the three.

triage.reason: The assertion is that a symbol declared in this module has zero readers in this module and carries a predicate no value of fleet.environment can satisfy. No artifact outside the repository can change a symbol's readership, so the rule does not reach this class of finding. Recorded so the bound is visible rather than implied: a load balancer terminating mTLS upstream would reduce the operational risk, and the docstring on lines 21-24 states the opposite arrangement ('the service terminates TLS itself'), but neither changes the fact that the declared control is never consulted.
The value is not consumed by name, by reflection or by a viper-style struct read: it is a Kotlin computed property on a data class, and a symbol search over an eight-file module is exhaustive.
Config.kt ships; the property exists in every build. The absence of a reader is not an absence from the artifact.

findings.title: Rate limiting is keyed on the peer address and does not cover the credential endpoint
findings.evidence: `requestKey { call -> call.request.local.remoteHost }` keys the 60-per-60s budget on the immediate TCP peer, not on the authenticated principal, and the routing block on lines 58-73 wraps only deviceRoutes, enrollmentRoutes and firmwareRoutes. tokenRoutes is registered on line 61, before the rateLimit block, and internalRoutes on line 72, after it — both unmetered. /oauth/token is where client secrets are verified (Token.kt:46).
findings.impact: Client secrets can be brute-forced without limit at /oauth/token. On the routes that are metered, any deployment behind a load balancer or ingress makes remoteHost the proxy's address, so all clients share one 60-request bucket: a single caller starves the fleet, and no per-client limit exists at all.
findings.recommendation: Key on the JWT subject where a principal exists and on the forwarded client address otherwise (install XForwardedHeaders and use call.request.origin.remoteHost), and register a separate, tighter limiter on /oauth/token keyed on client_id.

triage.reason: There is one RateLimit registration (lines 32-37) and one rateLimit scope (line 63); nothing else meters. Token.kt has no attempt counter or lockout.

An upstream gateway could rate-limit, but no gateway configuration exists in fleet-provision. UNKNOWN per FP-08. The keying defect is independent of it: remoteHost is read inside this process and is the proxy's address whenever a proxy exists.
This is not a redundant layer — no other limit on credential attempts exists in the module.

findings.title: The note update handler runs no authorization and loads the note by a client-supplied id
findings.evidence: Its sibling thirteen lines above does the check: handle_event("create_note", ...) wraps the write in `if Policy.can_write?(agent, ticket)` (line 58). update_note calls `Tickets.update_note(note_id, Sanitizer.sanitize_html(body))` with no policy call at all, and Tickets.update_note (tickets.ex:54-58) is `Repo.get!(Note, note_id) |> Note.changeset(...) |> Repo.update()` — a global lookup by primary key with no org scope, no ticket scope and no author check. note_id arrives in the event payload; the hidden input at ticket_live.html.heex:26 is a convenience for the browser, not a constraint, because a LiveView channel accepts whatever payload the client sends. Policy.can_write? explicitly denies auditors (policy.ex:19), and this path bypasses that denial too.
findings.impact: Any authenticated agent — including an auditor, whom the policy forbids from writing anything — rewrites the body of any note on any ticket in any organisation by naming its id. Combined with the sanitizer finding below, the rewritten body is also an XSS delivery vehicle into other agents' consoles.
findings.recommendation: Load the note through the caller's scope and check the policy before writing: fetch it via the ticket already on the socket, confirm `note.ticket_id == socket.assigns.ticket.id`, and gate on Policy.can_write?(agent, ticket) exactly as create_note does.

triage.reason: No layer between the event and Repo.update applies a scope. Note.changeset casts body_html only; the router pipeline established that an agent exists but not what that agent may write; the on_mount hook checks only for nil (require_agent.ex:25).
No external control is claimed for LiveView event authorization anywhere in this repository.

create_note and update_note reach the same effect on the same table — the body_html of a Note row — differing only in insert versus update. That is the sibling asymmetry, not two different operations.
note_id is a value in the event payload. Phoenix LiveView delivers whatever the socket sends; the rendered hidden field does not bound it.

findings.title: The ticket cache is keyed by id alone and returns rows the caller's scope excludes
findings.evidence: `Cache.fetch_ticket(id, fn -> Tickets.get_scoped(id, scope) end)` — the key passed to the cache is the bare ticket id and the scope lives only inside the closure. Cache.fetch_ticket (cache.ex:24-27) returns the stored value on any key match within the 60s TTL without calling the loader, so Tickets.apply_scope (tickets.ex:29-42) never runs for the second caller. The ETS table is `:named_table, :public` (cache.ex:15), shared by every LiveView process in the node. Both modules are correct read alone: get_scoped narrows properly for org, tenancy and :none, and the cache memoises exactly the key it is given. Nothing re-checks after the fetch — mount's case on lines 20-31 branches on nil versus a ticket and assigns it, and Policy.can_read?/visible? are never called anywhere (grep returns zero call sites).
findings.impact: An agent of org B opening /tickets/<id> within 60 seconds of an agent of org A opening the same id receives org A's ticket with its preloaded notes and attachments — the exact cross-tenancy read that org_scope/1 and apply_scope/2 exist to prevent. The reverse also holds: a negative result cached by a caller outside the scope is served to a caller inside it, hiding their own ticket for 60 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Put the scope in the key: `{:ticket, scope, id}`, or cache the unscoped row and apply the scope on every read. A cache whose loader closes over an authorization input must carry that input in its key.

triage.reason: The scope is applied only inside the loader, and cache.ex:25-26 returns before the loader runs. The router pipeline's ensure_agent (router.ex:64-68) checks that an agent exists, not which org's rows it may see.
The boundary is the org, made explicit by Policy.org_scope/1 (policy.ex:38-40) and enforced by apply_scope/2. Two agents of different orgs are two principals.
The cached value is a Ticket with :notes and :attachments preloaded (tickets.ex:17) — customer correspondence, which is the private content of the product.
Cache.init() is called unconditionally at the top of both mount clauses (lines 16 and 35) and the cache is on the default detail path.

findings.title: The escalate handler runs no authorization, including for the role the policy denies writes to
findings.evidence: `{:ok, ticket} = Tickets.escalate(socket.assigns.ticket, tier)` with no Policy.can_write? call, while create_note nineteen lines above makes exactly that call before writing (line 58). Tickets.escalate (tickets.ex:60-64) writes `tier` and `escalated_at` through Ticket.changeset with no check of its own, and `tier` is taken straight from the event payload — the select at ticket_live.html.heex:41-44 offers 2 and 3, but the channel accepts any value. Policy.can_write?(%{role: "auditor"}, _) returns false by an explicit clause (policy.ex:19); this path never consults it.
findings.impact: An auditor — a read-only compliance role by the policy's own definition — escalates tickets, and any agent escalates a ticket in a tenancy they can reach, with an arbitrary tier value written to the record. Escalation drives the SLA path, so this is a business-state change, not a cosmetic one.
findings.recommendation: Gate on Policy.can_write?(agent, ticket) as create_note does, and validate tier against the allowed set in Ticket.changeset rather than accepting the payload value.

triage.reason: Nothing between the event and Repo.update applies the policy: Ticket.changeset casts the attributes, the on_mount hook checks only for a nil agent, and the router pipeline ran only on the initial HTTP render.
escalate and create_note are both mutations on the same ticket reached from the same socket; one is gated and one is not.
There is no server-side equivalent elsewhere — Tickets.escalate/2 is the only implementation and it performs no check.

findings.title: Attachment routes sit outside the agent pipeline and the controller performs no authorization of its own
findings.evidence: The console scope pipes through `[:browser, :require_agent]` (line 24); the attachments scope pipes through `:browser` alone (line 38), so ensure_agent (lines 64-68) never runs for GET /attachments/:ticket_id/:filename or POST /attachments/:ticket_id. The controller then declines the job explicitly: its moduledoc (lines 5-8) says 'Attachment links are only rendered inside the ticket pane of the agent console, which the console pipeline already gates, so this controller is concerned with picking the right file rather than with who is asking.' That premise is false — this is a different scope with a different pipeline. Neither download/2 nor upload/2 reads conn.assigns.current_agent or calls Policy; both check only the shape of the identifiers (lines 46-53).
findings.impact: Anyone who learns a ticket UUID downloads that ticket's attachments with no session at all, and no ownership check applies even for a signed-in agent, so any agent reads any organisation's files. POST additionally writes an attacker-supplied file into priv/uploads/<uuid>/<name> with no size limit and no content check — protect_from_forgery requires a CSRF token, but an anonymous visitor mints one from GET /login, so it is a speed bump rather than an authorization control.
findings.recommendation: Add :require_agent to the attachments scope, and inside both actions load the ticket through Tickets.get_scoped(ticket_id, Policy.org_scope(agent)) and refuse when it comes back nil — so possession of a UUID is never sufficient. Add a size cap and an extension allowlist on upload.

triage.reason: The :browser pipeline (lines 9-17) ends at :load_agent, which only assigns current_agent and never halts; :ensure_agent lives in the separate :require_agent pipeline that this scope does not pipe through. The controller adds nothing — its two `with` chains check only the UUID and filename patterns.
Nothing frames these files as public. They are customer correspondence attachments served from a shared volume, linked only from the gated ticket pane (ticket_live.html.heex:51).
The boundary is the org, the same one Policy.org_scope/1 defines for tickets; the attachments belong to tickets that boundary already governs.
The benign reading is the moduledoc's own — that the console pipeline covers it. Router lines 23-24 and 37-38 show two distinct scopes with distinct pipe_through lists, so it does not.

findings.title: The HTML sanitizer is a four-pattern denylist and its output is rendered raw into the agent console
findings.evidence: sanitize_html removes exactly four things: paired
findings.impact: Customer-supplied email HTML, and any note body written through create_note or update_note, executes script in the agent console with the viewing agent's session — which, given the update_note finding, is a self-propagating path: an attacker rewrites a note, an agent views the ticket, the script runs with that agent's privileges.
findings.recommendation: Replace the denylist with an allowlist parser (html_sanitize_ex's :basic_html or an equivalent that parses rather than pattern-matches), keep the tables and lists the moduledoc wants, and drop every attribute not on the list. Escaping by regex over HTML cannot be made correct.

triage.reason: sanitize_html is the only sanitisation on the path and raw/1 removes the framework's escaping. No CSP header is set anywhere in the tree — put_secure_browser_headers (router.ex:15) sets X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy but no content-security-policy.
The input is the HTML part of an inbound customer email (moduledoc lines 2-4) and the note bodies posted through the console — both external.
The sink is raw/1 inside a HEEx template rendered as text/html; the surviving constructs are executable markup, not text.
No CSP and no other layer bounds the impact, so the severity is not reduced to informational; the payload runs with agent privileges in the console origin.

findings.title: The sort parameter is converted to an atom with String.to_atom on every navigation
findings.evidence: `defp sort_key(value), do: String.to_atom(value)` is called from handle_params (line 47) with `params["sort"]`, i.e. the URL query string, on every mount and every live navigation. String.to_atom creates a new atom for any string it has not seen. Atoms are never garbage-collected in the BEAM and the default limit is 1,048,576; the safe primitive, String.to_existing_atom, is not used and no allowlist narrows the value first. Compare billing-portal's parseSort (invoices.controller.ts:19-23), which faces the same problem and answers it with a membership test against a frozen tuple.
findings.impact: A caller requesting /tickets?sort=<distinct value> in a loop exhausts the atom table and terminates the BEAM node, taking the whole helpdesk console down. No credential-specific privilege is required beyond reaching the route.
findings.recommendation: Match against an explicit list of sortable columns and fall back to :inserted_at, or use String.to_existing_atom inside a rescue. Never build an atom from request data.

triage.reason: No allowlist or pattern constrains params["sort"] before line 51; sort_key/1 has two clauses and the nil clause is the only guard.
The value is the sort query parameter, read directly in handle_params.

The harm is exhaustion of a fixed global table, not execution or re-parsing at a sink. The resulting atom is stored in an assign and is not used to build a query, so there is no injection component — list_scoped/2 is called with the literal :inserted_at (line 42).
handle_params is an @impl callback on the shipped LiveView, reached on every one of the five live routes.

findings.title: The LiveView mount guard lists live actions the router does not register and omits the ones it does
findings.evidence: @guarded is [:edit, :delete, :new]. The router registers exactly five live actions in this live_session: :index, :show, :edit, :escalate and :assign (router.ex:27-31). Two of the three guarded names, :delete and :new, exist nowhere in the router, and the two mutating actions that do exist — :escalate and :assign — are absent from the list, so line 22's `socket.assigns.live_action not in @guarded` returns true for them and the hook conts with a nil agent. The moduledoc (lines 4-8) states the purpose the list defeats: 'The router pipeline covers the first HTTP render. This hook is what keeps the mutating actions honest on a socket that reconnects without replaying the pipeline.'
findings.impact: Bounded, which is why this is low. The hook adds nothing beyond the router pipeline for four of the five actions, and for the fifth it duplicates it. It does not by itself open unauthenticated access, because Phoenix mints the LiveView session token during the gated static render, and mount/3 with a nil agent resolves org_scope to :none, which apply_scope turns into `where false`. The cost is that a control the module documents as covering socket reconnection covers almost nothing, and it reads as present — which is exactly what made it worth writing down beside the cache finding, whose exploitation would otherwise be blocked here.
findings.recommendation: Derive the guarded set from the router rather than restating it, or invert it — guard every action except an explicit read-only allowlist — so a new live action is protected by default instead of by remembering to add it. Check authorization, not merely non-nil-ness.

triage.reason: The hook is the only control that runs on a socket reconnect; the router pipeline does not replay on a channel join, which the moduledoc itself states.
There is no reading on which :delete and :new are live actions here — the live_session block (router.ex:26-32) is the complete list, and neither name appears in it or in TicketLive.

The router pipeline (:require_agent, router.ex:24) answers the same question — is there an agent — on the initial HTTP render, and Phoenix's signed session token means a socket cannot be joined without having passed it. The impact therefore does not reach the user on its own, so this is bounded rather than deleted: it is written down at low severity because it is the defence-in-depth layer the moduledoc claims, and it is not doing the job it claims.

findings.title: Kafka message headers are unpickled before any signature check, on every message from the whole ledger namespace
findings.evidence: decode_context calls `pickle.loads(value)` on the raw bytes of the `x-ctx` header. consumer.py:51 calls it for every message, and it runs *before* apply_transfer on line 54, which is the only place verify() is reached. The signature covers `msg.value()` and nothing else: app.py:53 computes `sign(value)` over the encoded payload, so the headers travel unauthenticated even for topics whose policy sets require_signature=True. The consumer subscribes by pattern to `^ledger\..*` (topics.py:46, consumer.py:67), so every topic in the namespace — including ledger.dlq.v1 — feeds this call. The value payload uses json (serde.py:10-15); only the trace context uses pickle, and the comment on lines 18-19 explains why it was chosen, not what it costs.
findings.impact: Pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes code during reconstruction, so a crafted x-ctx header is remote code execution in the ledger worker process — the process that holds the signing key and the ledger database — reached before the integrity control that would have stopped a forged message.
findings.recommendation: Encode the trace context as JSON like the value, or use a schema-bound format. If pickle must stay, cover the headers with the HMAC and verify before decoding — but the ordering fix alone is not sufficient, because pickle remains unsafe for any data an attacker can influence.

triage.reason: The HMAC is computed over the value only (app.py:47-53) and is verified inside apply_transfer at apply.py:42, three lines after decode_context has already run. No control precedes line 51.
The sink is pickle.loads, which the pack names as the canonical format that reconstructs arbitrary objects. It is not a parser.

Whether an outside party can produce to a ledger.* topic depends on broker ACLs, which are not in this repository — no broker configuration, no ACL file, no topic provisioning. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, and it is what caps this at probable. What would settle it: the Kafka ACLs for the ledger.* prefix, particularly for ledger.dlq.v1. Note that the intake service (api/app.py) publishes on behalf of external clients, so the value path already carries outside influence into the namespace.
Producer and consumer are separate services with separate deployments, and the intake API is a client-facing HTTP service — the trust domains are not the same.

findings.title: The dead-letter replay path disables signature verification and takes its policy and its org from unsigned headers
findings.evidence: replay_one calls apply_transfer with `verify_signature=False`, which short-circuits the first conjunct of apply.py:42 so verify() never runs regardless of the topic policy. The policy itself comes from `policy_for(original_topic)` where original_topic is `header_value(headers, "x-original-topic") or DLQ_TOPIC` (line 38) — an unauthenticated header, defaulting to 'ledger.dlq.v1', which is absent from TOPIC_POLICY and therefore resolves to OPEN_POLICY with allow_account_override=True. consumer_org likewise comes from the unsigned `x-org` header (line 54). The is_admin_topic gate that consumer.py:43 applies has no counterpart here, so a header of `x-original-topic: ledger.admin.adjustments.v1` selects the 100,000,000-cent ceiling with no PLATFORM_ORGS check. The docstring's premise (lines 3-5) — 'They were already accepted by the intake service and checked by the main consumer before being parked' — is not met by this codebase: consumer.py never produces to the DLQ; on failure it logs (line 92) and commits (line 93).
findings.impact: A message placed on ledger.dlq.v1 posts ledger entries with no signature, no account-ownership check (allow_account_override is on), and the topic ceiling of the attacker's choosing. The only surviving constraint is DAILY_ACCOUNT_LIMIT_CENTS (apply.py:55), 2,000,000 cents per account per day — four times what the transfers topic permits per message and applied per account, so it is a rate rather than an authorisation.
findings.recommendation: Verify the signature on replay too — a message that was legitimately parked still carries its original x-sig over the same value bytes. Take the original topic from a signed field inside the payload rather than from a header, and apply the same is_admin_topic gate the main consumer applies.

triage.reason: verify_signature=False removes the only integrity control, and the ownership check at apply.py:51 is disabled by allow_account_override, which the attacker selects via the topic header. No compensating check exists in replay_one.
x-original-topic and x-org are Kafka headers set by whoever produced the message; the HMAC covers only msg.value().

Produce rights to ledger.dlq.v1 depend on broker ACLs not present in this repository — the same bound as the deserialization finding, and what caps this at probable. What would settle it: the ACL for ledger.dlq.v1. The code-level bypass is confirmed from retry.py:38, :54 and :55 alone.

The benign reading is the docstring's — that these messages were already checked. Nothing in the tree writes to the DLQ, so what a message on that topic has been through is not established by this codebase; and even a legitimately parked message retains a verifiable signature that this path chooses not to check.

findings.title: Any topic without an explicit entry inherits a policy with no signature requirement and account override enabled
findings.evidence: policy_for (line 50) is `TOPIC_POLICY.get(topic, OPEN_POLICY)`, and OPEN_POLICY is require_signature=False, max_amount_cents=10,000,000 and allow_account_override=True — strictly more permissive on all three axes than every named entry: twenty times the transfers ceiling (500,000, line 30), signature not required where all three named topics require it, and account override enabled where the two customer topics disable it. Only three topics are named. Consumers subscribe by pattern (`^ledger\..*`, line 46) precisely so a new stream needs no deploy, which the consumer docstring restates (consumer.py:2-4) — so the set of topics reaching this default is open-ended by design. The default is already load-bearing today: ledger.dlq.v1 is not in TOPIC_POLICY, so the retry path's default topic resolves here.
findings.impact: Every stream someone adds to the namespace, and the dead-letter topic that already exists, is processed with the relaxed profile. The comment on lines 18-20 explains the reasoning — new streams are 'internal fan-out of already-validated events' — but the mechanism grants the permissive profile to any topic name at all, including one an attacker creates where auto-topic-creation is on.
findings.recommendation: Make the fallback the strictest profile, not the loosest: require_signature=True, allow_account_override=False and the lowest ceiling, so an unregistered topic fails closed. Better still, refuse to process a topic with no explicit entry and alert.

triage.reason: policy_for is the single source of the three flags, and both consumers use it (consumer.py:47, retry.py:50). No layer re-imposes a signature requirement or an ownership check on top of it.
The default is not hypothetical: ledger.dlq.v1 is a topic this codebase names and subscribes to (retry.py:21, :68) and it is absent from TOPIC_POLICY, so policy_for returns OPEN_POLICY for it today.
The comment frames it as inheritance by internal fan-out, but the lookup keys on nothing that distinguishes an internal fan-out topic from any other string.
An intended, bounded relaxation would name the topics it relaxes. This one applies to the complement of a three-entry set.

findings.title: The message signing key falls back to a value published in the source file when the environment variable is unset
findings.evidence: `SIGNING_KEY = os.environ.get("LEDGER_SIGNING_KEY", DEFAULT_SIGNING_KEY)` with DEFAULT_SIGNING_KEY = 'ledger-stream-dev-signing-key' on line 8. The module resolves the key at import time and never asserts that the environment supplied one, so a deployment that omits the variable signs and verifies with a value anyone reading this repository holds — and does so silently, since sign() and verify() behave identically either way. The same project family shows the correct shape one service over: fleet-provision's Config.kt:34-37 reads its signing secret and then `require(secret.isNotBlank())`, failing at boot rather than at the first request, which is what its own comment on lines 6-8 says the design intends.
findings.impact: Where the variable is unset, `x-sig` is forgeable by anyone with the repository, which removes the only integrity control on the two topics that require a signature — transfers up to 500,000 cents and holds up to 250,000 — and lets a forged message satisfy apply.py:42.
findings.recommendation: Delete the fallback and raise at import when LEDGER_SIGNING_KEY is absent, so a misconfigured deployment cannot start. Rotate the value if it has ever been used anywhere real.

triage.reason: The literal is not a placeholder of the ${VAR}/changeme kind that would be inert: it is a usable HMAC key, and sign() at line 15 will happily use it.
signing.py ships as the module both consumers and the intake API import; the fallback is unconditional, not selected by a build or a flag.

The comment on line 7 says the value is 'Overridden per environment by the deploy manifest.' No manifest, chart, compose file or environment definition is present anywhere in ledger-stream, so per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN and this finding is capped at probable. What would settle it: the deploy manifest for the worker and the intake service. The defect that the module fails open instead of refusing to start is confirmed from lines 8 and 10 regardless of what any manifest sets.

findings.title: The admin-topic gate authorises on an unsigned Kafka header while the signed field beside it is used only as a preference
findings.evidence: `if is_admin_topic(topic) and org_id not in PLATFORM_ORGS` where org_id is `header_value(headers, "x-org")` (line 41) — a Kafka header. The HMAC at app.py:53 is computed over `value` only, so headers are outside the integrity envelope. The payload does carry an org_id that *is* covered by the signature (app.py:70 writes it into the payload before encode_value at line 47), but apply.py:61 uses it only as `payload.get("org_id") or consumer_org` for labelling the stored entry, and the header value is what both the admin gate (line 43) and the account-ownership check (apply.py:51-52, via consumer_org) actually consult. The authenticated field and the field the controls read are different fields.
findings.impact: The single gate protecting ledger.admin.adjustments.v1 — the topic with the 100,000,000-cent ceiling and allow_account_override enabled — is satisfied by setting a header to 'org_platform'. The per-account ownership check on non-admin topics is likewise satisfied by naming the owning org in a header.
findings.recommendation: Read the org from the signed payload, not from the header, and verify the signature before any policy decision — including before the admin gate. If a header must remain for routing, treat it as a hint and cross-check it against the signed value.

triage.reason: The signature verification that could have bound the header runs later (apply.py:42) and covers a different byte range (raw_value). Nothing else validates x-org.
x-org is a producer-set header carried through header_value, which decodes with errors='replace' and applies no pattern.

Broker ACLs could restrict who produces to ledger.admin.*, which would bound this, but no ACL configuration is in this repository. UNKNOWN per FP-08, and it is what caps this at probable. What would settle it: the ACL for the ledger.admin. prefix. The mismatch between the authenticated field and the consulted field is confirmed from consumer.py:41-43 and app.py:47-56.
PLATFORM_ORGS is the only control on the admin topic (its comment on line 23 says so), not a redundant layer.

findings.title: The settlement backfill writes ledger entries with none of the policy checks the consumer path applies
findings.evidence: The `entries` table has two writers. post_entry (line 62) is reached only from apply_transfer, which runs four checks first: signature (apply.py:42), amount sign and topic ceiling (46), account ownership (51), and the daily account limit (55). append_raw runs `INSERT OR REPLACE` over rows built by backfill.rows_from (backfill.py:34-45), which applies `int()` to amount_cents and nothing else — no sign test, no ceiling, no daily limit, no ownership check — and takes org_id from the CSV with `record.get("org_id") or org_id`, so a row selects its own organisation. Because the primary key is the caller-supplied `record.get("entry_id")` and the statement is INSERT OR REPLACE, a row silently overwrites an existing ledger entry rather than conflicting with it. post_entry's own docstring (line 63) states the assumption — 'Callers are expected to have run the policy checks' — which is true of one caller and false of the other.
findings.impact: A settlement export can post negative or arbitrarily large amounts, attribute entries to any organisation, and replace existing ledger rows by reusing their ids — bypassing every invariant the streaming path enforces, in the ledger of record.
findings.recommendation: Route the backfill through the same validation: reject non-positive amounts, apply the ceiling and the daily limit, pin org_id to the --org argument rather than letting the file override it, and use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING so a replay cannot rewrite history.

triage.reason: Nothing between the CSV reader and executemany validates: rows_from yields tuples, load() lists them, append_raw writes them. resolve_export (line 26) constrains which file is read, not what is in it.
Both writers target the same seven columns of the same `entries` table with the same statement shape; they differ only in the checks that precede them.
The file is produced by the settlement bank (docstring lines 3-4), a third party, so there is a second principal even though the tool runs on an operator jumpbox.

Who may write into the drop directory is a deployment property — the docstring says it is mounted read only on the jumpbox, which describes the reader's access and not the writer's. Not evidenced here, so UNKNOWN, and it caps this at probable. What would settle it: the mount definition and the transfer mechanism that populates /mnt/settlement. The writer asymmetry itself is confirmed.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled Kafka headers reach a line-oriented log with no neutralisation
findings.evidence: log_escaper.py reported 8 uncleared logging arguments in this tree; three carry values that come straight off the wire. consumer.py:44 logs `org_id` from `header_value(headers, "x-org")`, and retry.py:41 and :61 log `original_topic` from `header_value(headers, "x-original-topic")`. header_value (serde.py:34) decodes with `errors="replace"`, which substitutes only undecodable bytes — carriage return and newline are valid UTF-8 and pass through untouched. No escaper, allowlist or pattern sits between the header and the logger, and no logging configuration exists anywhere in ledger-stream, so the default line-oriented format applies. The line at consumer.py:44 is the audit record for a *rejected* admin-topic message, which is the record an attacker most wants to control.
findings.impact: A header containing CRLF followed by a plausible record forges log entries: one input, two records. Where an aggregator parses by line, the forged record is indistinguishable from a real one, so the evidence that a non-platform org attempted an admin-topic write can be buried under fabricated successes.
findings.recommendation: Log through a structured handler that escapes control characters and parse it as structured on the other end, or neutralise the value at the call site — the header is an opaque identifier, so an anchored pattern test before logging costs nothing.

triage.reason: The values are Kafka headers set by the producer and are not constrained by any pattern before the call; header_value returns whatever decoded string arrives.

Whether the sink re-parses or renders depends on the handler and the aggregator, and neither is configured anywhere in this repository — logging.getLogger is called with no basicConfig, no dictConfig and no handler. Per the procedure this distinction is the whole triage, so I will not assert it; it caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the logging configuration and whether the aggregator parses by line or by JSON object.
The %s form is not an exculpation — deferred interpolation and concatenation reach the sink identically, which is the measured reason the tool ignores the idiom.
Even where the sink cannot execute, the accountability loss on a rejection record remains, so this does not fall to informational.

findings.title: The transfer intake service asserts an organisation boundary that no middleware implements
findings.evidence: _org_of returns `request["org_id"]` and its docstring says 'Resolved by the auth middleware from the verified workspace token.' build_app (lines 100-104) constructs `web.Application()` with no middlewares argument, adds routes and returns — nothing in this tree sets request["org_id"], and no middleware, decorator or signature verification appears anywhere under ledger-stream/api. The module docstring (lines 3-4) states the model being relied on: 'Clients authenticate with a workspace JWT and POST a transfer.' The org value that _org_of returns is stamped into the payload (lines 70, 84) and becomes the signed org_id the consumer stores.
findings.impact: As written the two POST routes raise KeyError and return 500, so the service fails closed rather than open — the practical impact is that the intake path does not work. The finding is that the trust boundary the whole pipeline depends on is asserted by a comment: whatever supplies org_id is not reviewable here, and if a wrapper sets it from a client-supplied header rather than a verified token, every downstream ownership decision inherits that.
findings.recommendation: Install the authentication middleware in build_app so the boundary is visible at the composition root, verify the workspace JWT against the JWKS, and set request["org_id"] only from a verified claim. Add a test that an unauthenticated POST returns 401 rather than 500.

triage.reason: There is no middleware in the application object, and the two handlers call _org_of directly with no other check (lines 68 and 82).

The middleware may be installed by a deployment wrapper or an ASGI/gateway layer outside these ten files — build_app is exported and could be composed elsewhere. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS, and it caps this at probable. What would settle it: the entry point that actually serves build_app() in the deployment, and whether it adds middlewares.
