This is not a redundant layer: org_id is the only tenancy input the pipeline has, and apply.py:51 and :61 both consume what it produces.

findings.title: The partner virtual host neither strips the identity headers nor runs the session check
findings.evidence: public_vh declares `request_headers_to_remove: [x-fleet-user, x-fleet-roles, x-fleet-tenant]` (lines 63-66) under a comment stating the invariant — 'Identity is stamped by sessiond, never by the client.' partner_vh declares no such list, and additionally disables the ext_authz filter for its routes with `typed_per_filter_config: envoy.filters.http.ext_authz: {disabled: true}` (lines 78-81). Behind it, principalFrom (service/auth.go:22-37) builds the entire Principal — user, tenant and roles — from those three headers with no other source, and HasRole (line 41) treats a role of 'admin' as satisfying every check. The listener is plain HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8080 with no transport_socket (lines 8-9), so virtual-host selection comes from the client's Host header; nothing in this configuration binds `domains: ["partners.example.com"]` to a client certificate. The RBAC filter above does not cover it either: its permissions are /internal/ and /admin/ only (lines 27-28), and partner_vh routes /v1/.
findings.impact: A request to the edge with `Host: partners.example.com` and self-asserted `X-Fleet-User`, `X-Fleet-Tenant: <victim>` and `X-Fleet-Roles: admin` passes ext_authz (disabled), keeps its headers (not stripped), and is accepted by the object service as that tenant's administrator — full read and write of any tenant's objects with no credential. Both files are correct in isolation: the Go service is right to trust headers behind a proxy that strips them, and a partner host authenticated by mTLS is a reasonable design.
findings.recommendation: Add the same request_headers_to_remove list to partner_vh — identity headers must be stripped on every virtual host, without exception — and derive the partner identity from the validated client certificate (an ext_authz service or a header the LB sets from the cert and Envoy re-stamps), not from headers the client supplies.

triage.reason: No layer between the partner route and the Go handler removes the headers or re-derives identity: ext_authz is disabled per-route, the RBAC filter's permissions do not include /v1/, and the object service has no verification of its own (auth.go has no signature, token or certificate check).

The comment on lines 75-77 claims partners terminate mTLS at the load balancer. No load-balancer configuration is present in this repository, and even granting it, nothing shown maps a verified client certificate onto the x-fleet-* headers or prevents a partner from asserting another tenant's id. Per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN, which caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the LB configuration and whether it strips or overwrites x-fleet-* on the partner path. The header-stripping asymmetry between the two virtual hosts is confirmed from lines 63-66 and 73-86 regardless.
An intended, bounded exposure would still confine a partner to its own tenant. x-fleet-tenant is the only thing that selects the tenant, and the partner supplies it.

findings.title: The object service publishes its port on the host, so every control in the proxy is optional
findings.evidence: `objects` declares `ports: - "8081:8081"`, publishing the service on the Docker host alongside the edge proxy's own 8080. The contrast inside the same file settles the intent: `sessiond` (lines 32-38) declares no ports and is reachable only on the mesh network, which is the correct shape for a service that should only be spoken to from inside. Every control this service depends on lives in the proxy — the RBAC DENY policy for /internal/ and /admin/ (envoy.yaml:21-33), the ext_authz session check (lines 34-53), and the identity-header stripping (lines 63-66) — and the Go service implements none of them: handleAdmin (admin.go:22), handleStats, handleDiag and handleResolve call no requireRole, and principalFrom trusts the headers it is given.
findings.impact: Anyone who reaches the Docker host on 8081 talks to the object service directly with self-asserted identity headers and no proxy in the path: /admin dumps the cross-tenant metadata snapshot and restores arbitrary objects, /internal/diag executes shell commands, /internal/resolve and /internal/stats answer, and /v1/objects/* is read and written as any tenant. The proxy's entire security configuration is bypassed by choosing a different port.
findings.recommendation: Remove the ports mapping from `objects` and let it be reachable only over the `mesh` network, exactly as `sessiond` already is. If a direct debugging path is needed, bind it to 127.0.0.1 explicitly (`127.0.0.1:8081:8081`) rather than to all interfaces.

triage.reason: The Go service enforces nothing on its own: auth.go derives the principal from headers, and the three /internal handlers and handleAdmin call requireRole zero times. Only the two /v1/objects branches call it (main.go:58, 76), and those trust the same headers.

This is not the intended public entry point — the edge proxy on 8080 is, and depends_on (lines 11-13) places objects behind it. The pack's exculpation for a public balancer moves the finding to what sits behind it; here what sits behind it is published too.
A published port is reachable from outside the container's trust domain by definition; sessiond in the same file shows what 'internal only' looks like in this compose file.
No external firewall is claimed anywhere in this repository for port 8081, and the compose file is the artifact that decides the binding.

findings.title: The connectivity probe passes a query parameter into a shell command line
findings.evidence: `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", "ping -c 1 -W 2 "+host).CombinedOutput()` where `host` is `r.URL.Query().Get("host")` (line 15). The only test on the value is that it is non-empty (line 16); no allowlist, no character filter, no hostname validation. The shell is explicit, so every metacharacter is live, and CombinedOutput returns stdout and stderr in the JSON response (line 28), making it a direct output channel rather than a blind one. The 5-second context timeout bounds duration, not what runs. The sibling handler one function down shows the right shape: handleResolve (line 44) uses net.DefaultResolver.LookupHost with no shell at all.
findings.impact: `GET /internal/diag?host=x;id` executes arbitrary commands as the service user inside the objects container and returns their output in the response body — remote code execution with a read-back channel, on a container that holds the objects-data volume. Reachable directly on the published port 8081 per the previous finding.
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell: `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "ping", "-c", "1", "-W", "2", host)` passes the value as one argv element that no shell interprets. Validate `host` as a hostname or IP first, and gate the endpoint with requireRole.

triage.reason: Nothing validates or escapes between the query parameter and the command string. handleDiag calls no requireRole, and the Envoy RBAC that nominally covers /internal/ is bypassed by the published port and, for /admin, by the prefix mismatch reported separately.
The value is r.URL.Query().Get("host"), read on line 15 and concatenated on line 24 with nothing in between.
There is no reading on which `sh -c` with a concatenated string is not a shell: the argv is literally ["sh", "-c", <string>], which is the pack's exact vulnerable pattern for Go.
The handler is registered on the same mux as the tenant-facing object API (main.go:120) on a published port, so an outside caller is a second principal.

findings.title: The response cache is keyed on the request path alone and sits in front of every authorization check
findings.class: Cross-tenant disclosure through a shared cache
findings.evidence: `key := r.URL.Path` — no tenant, no user, no Vary, no method beyond the GET filter. main.go:125 installs it as `Handler: withCache(srv.cache, mux)`, so the cache wraps the mux: on a hit, cache.go:82-92 writes the stored status, headers and body and returns before ServeHTTP is ever called, which means requireRole (main.go:58) and the `meta.Tenant != p.Tenant` check (line 67) do not run. Any 200 GET is stored (line 97). Read separately, each file is sound: handleObject checks the tenant on every read, and the cache memoises what it is told to. The paths that get cached are exactly the sensitive ones — /v1/objects/<key> (another tenant's object bytes), /v1/objects/ (List(p.Tenant), the caller's own listing), and /admin (adminOverview's full cross-tenant metadata snapshot, admin.go:47-55).
findings.impact: For the 20-second TTL (main.go:36), a request with no identity headers at all receives the previous caller's private response: another tenant's object body and checksum, another tenant's object listing, or the whole store's metadata from /admin. This bypasses authentication, not merely tenant scoping.
findings.recommendation: Include the principal in the key — tenant and roles at minimum — or, better, place the cache inside the handler after authorization rather than in front of the mux, and never cache a response whose content depends on the caller. Add a hard exclusion for /admin and /internal.

triage.reason: The compensating control exists and is unreachable on a hit: requireRole and the tenant comparison live inside handleObject, and withCache returns at cache.go:91 without entering next.ServeHTTP.
The tenant is the boundary the service is built around — ObjectMeta.Tenant, Store.List(tenant), the errNotOwner sentinel — and the cache serves across it.
The cached bodies are tenant object contents and the admin metadata snapshot, not public content.
withCache is the shipped top-level handler; no flag disables it and newResponseCache is constructed unconditionally at main.go:110.

findings.title: The RBAC policy's /admin/ prefix does not match the /admin path the service actually registers
findings.evidence: The DENY policy's permissions are `url_path: {path: {prefix: "/internal/"}}` and `url_path: {path: {prefix: "/admin/"}}` — both with a trailing slash. The Go service registers `mux.HandleFunc("/admin", srv.handleAdmin)` (main.go:118) with no trailing slash, which in net/http is an exact-match pattern: it serves /admin and only /admin, and creates no subtree, so /admin/ is a 404. `/admin` does not have the prefix `/admin/`, so the policy never matches the only URL this surface answers on. The /internal/ entry is correct by contrast — the three internal handlers are registered as /internal/stats, /internal/diag and /internal/resolve (main.go:119-121), all of which do carry the prefix. One character, and the two files are each internally consistent.
findings.impact: The control that confines the operator surface to the mesh subnet does not cover the operator surface. Requests to /admin from outside 10.20.0.0/16 pass the RBAC filter; handleAdmin then performs no role check of its own, so a GET returns the full cross-tenant metadata snapshot and a POST reaches restore, purge-cache and usage.
findings.recommendation: Match the exact path as well as the subtree — add `url_path: {path: {exact: "/admin"}}` alongside the prefix entry — and add a test that asserts the deny applies to every path the mux registers. Do not rely on a prefix to cover a route registered without a trailing slash.

triage.reason: The RBAC filter is the only network-origin control on this path, and handleAdmin (admin.go:22-45) calls no requireRole. ext_authz still runs for public_vh, so a valid session is needed there — but a valid session is not staff, and the RBAC filter is what was meant to distinguish them.

Envoy's url_path prefix matcher is a literal string prefix on the path; '/admin' does not begin with '/admin/'. And Go's ServeMux does not redirect /admin to /admin/ for a pattern registered without the trailing slash — the implicit redirect runs the other way, from /admin to /admin/ only when '/admin/' is the registered subtree pattern.
Both the filter and the /admin route ship: envoy.yaml is mounted read-only into the edge container (docker-compose.yml:8) and main.go:118 registers the handler unconditionally.

findings.title: The entire operator surface runs with no role check, unlike every object route beside it
findings.evidence: handleAdmin is the whole operator surface by its own comment (lines 19-21) and never calls requireRole, principalFrom or HasRole — grep for requireRole in mesh-gateway/service returns three sites: the definition in auth.go:52 and two call sites in main.go, both inside handleObject (lines 58 and 76). Every branch of handleAdmin is therefore reached on identity alone: a non-POST request falls through to adminOverview (line 24), which writes the complete Store.Snapshot() — every tenant's ObjectMeta, keys, owners, sizes and checksums; `usage` returns Store.List(req.Tenant) for any tenant named in the body (line 41), which is the sibling of a route that pins the tenant to the authenticated principal; `purge-cache` empties the cache; `restore` writes objects. The asymmetry is exact: the same process gates GET and PUT on /v1/objects with requireRole and leaves the surface that reads across all of them ungated.
findings.impact: Any caller who reaches /admin — which, per the RBAC prefix mismatch and the published port, includes callers from outside the mesh — enumerates every tenant's objects, reads any tenant's listing by naming it in the body, and reaches the restore path.
findings.recommendation: Call requireRole(w, r, "admin") at the top of handleAdmin and derive the tenant for the `usage` action from the authenticated principal rather than from req.Tenant, matching what handleObject already does.

triage.reason: No in-process layer covers it: the only middleware is withCache (main.go:125), which caches rather than authorizes, and there is no base handler or interceptor. The out-of-process layer that was supposed to cover it is the RBAC policy whose prefix does not match this path.

The claimed out-of-process control is the Envoy RBAC filter, and it is not outside this repository — envoy.yaml is in the tree and mounted into the edge container at docker-compose.yml:8. The evidence therefore arrived, and it shows the control does not cover this path: its permissions are the prefixes /internal/ and /admin/ (lines 27-28), and the registered route is /admin with no trailing slash. An exculpation whose artifact is present and negative is DOES_NOT_HOLD, not UNKNOWN.
handleAdmin and handleObject reach comparable effects on the same store — listing and writing objects — and one calls requireRole while the other does not.
Store.Snapshot returns the metadata of every tenant (store.go:122-126), so the response crosses the tenant boundary the rest of the service maintains.

findings.title: putRaw writes the object store without the ownership and quota checks Put enforces, from a client-supplied metadata block
findings.evidence: Two writers reach s.meta and the blob file. Put (line 52) refuses to overwrite another tenant's key (`existing.Tenant != meta.Tenant` → errNotOwner, lines 56-58), enforces the quota (line 59), and computes Size and Checksum from the body it was handed (lines 63-65) rather than trusting them. putRaw does none of that — it goes straight to writeBlob and then assigns s.meta[meta.Key] = meta. Its caller is restoreSnapshot (admin.go:58-68), which iterates `req.Objects` from the request body, and adminEntry embeds ObjectMeta whole (admin.go:14-17), so Key, Tenant, Owner, Size and Checksum all come from the JSON the caller sends. handleAdmin performs no role check, so the path is reachable by whoever reaches /admin. The docstring on lines 76-77 states the assumption — 'the metadata comes from a previous export of this same store' — which the HTTP handler does not verify in any way.
findings.impact: A POST to /admin with action 'restore' overwrites any tenant's object with attacker-chosen bytes while claiming any Tenant and Owner, sets an arbitrary Checksum that the GET path returns to clients in X-Object-Checksum (main.go:72) without recomputing it, and bypasses the quota entirely. It also poisons the in-memory usage accounting (line 85) with a length the caller influences.
findings.recommendation: Have restoreSnapshot call Put rather than putRaw so both paths share one set of checks, recompute Size and Checksum from the body on every write, and verify the snapshot's integrity — a signature over the export — before trusting its metadata.

triage.reason: Nothing between the JSON decode at admin.go:29 and putRaw at line 61 validates the metadata; handleAdmin runs no authorization and restoreSnapshot only counts successes.
Put and putRaw write the same map and the same blob path via the same writeBlob helper (line 82 and line 67); they differ only in the checks that precede the write, which is exactly the asymmetry.
ObjectMeta is decoded from the request body through an embedded struct field, so every one of its fields is caller-supplied.
A restore endpoint intended for operator use would still be bounded by authentication and by verification of the export; neither is present.

findings.title: The RBAC filter's trusted-subnet principal is the same subnet a published port's translated source address falls inside
findings.evidence: The DENY policy fires only for a principal whose direct_remote_ip is NOT inside 10.20.0.0/16 (lines 30-33). docker-compose.yml:43-47 defines the mesh network with exactly that subnet, and lines 9-10 publish the edge listener as `8080:8080`. Where the Docker daemon runs with the userland proxy enabled — its default on many installations — traffic arriving on the published port is forwarded into the container by docker-proxy, and the source address the container observes is the bridge gateway (10.20.0.1 for this network), which is inside 10.20.0.0/16. direct_remote_ip is the actual TCP peer and is not affected by `use_remote_address: true` (line 16), which governs X-Forwarded-For handling rather than the connection's source. In that configuration every externally-originated request presents an in-subnet peer address and the deny never applies.
findings.impact: The one control confining /internal/ and /admin/ to the mesh would be inert for all external traffic, exposing the internal handlers — including the command-injection probe — to anyone who can reach port 8080. Where the daemon runs with userland-proxy disabled, DNAT preserves the original source and the control works as intended: the outcome depends on a daemon setting, not on this configuration.
findings.recommendation: Do not express a trust boundary as an IP range that a NAT hop can land inside. Authorize the operator surface with a credential — an ext_authz policy or mTLS — and keep the subnet rule as defence in depth. At minimum, verify the observed direct_remote_ip for external traffic in the actual deployment.

triage.reason: No other control covers /internal/: the Go handlers call no requireRole, and ext_authz authorizes a session rather than asserting operator status.

Whether the source address is rewritten depends on the Docker daemon's userland-proxy setting and on whether an upstream LB terminates the connection — neither is in this repository, and per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. It is what caps this at probable. What would settle it: `docker info` for the daemon's userland proxy setting, or one request from off-host with Envoy's RBAC logging enabled to read the observed direct_remote_ip.

The RBAC construct itself is written correctly — DENY with a negated principal is the right idiom — so the benign reading of the YAML is not available; the problem is the value of the range, not the shape of the rule.

findings.title: The diagnostic resolver answers arbitrary DNS lookups from the service's network position
findings.evidence: `net.DefaultResolver.LookupHost(ctx, name)` with `name` taken from the query string (line 35) and no allowlist. The response reports whether resolution succeeded and how many addresses came back (lines 45-49). The handler calls no requireRole and is registered at main.go:121 on the mux that the published port 8081 exposes directly.
findings.impact: An outside caller enumerates internal DNS names — service discovery entries, internal hostnames — by observing which resolve, and triggers lookups against attacker-controlled domains, giving a low-bandwidth out-of-band channel. No connection is made and only a count is returned, which is why this is low rather than an SSRF.
findings.recommendation: Gate it with requireRole and restrict the names to a configured allowlist of upstreams the operator actually diagnoses.

triage.reason: The value is r.URL.Query().Get("name"), passed to the resolver two lines later.

The sink is a live DNS resolution performed by the service process against a name the caller chooses, so the lookup genuinely happens; what is bounded is what comes back, which is FP-10's question rather than this one.

The sink resolves and does not dial: the comment on lines 32-33 is accurate and the handler returns only len(addrs), so no response body, port or content from the target reaches the caller. That bounds the impact to name enumeration and an out-of-band signal, which is why it is written down at low severity rather than reported as SSRF. FP-10 downgrades; it does not delete.

findings.title: Container images are not pinned by digest and the proxy image uses a moving tag
findings.evidence: `image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30-latest` is a moving tag by construction — the same reference resolves to different content over time — and `ghcr.io/example/sessiond:2.4.1` (line 33) is a mutable version tag rather than an immutable `@sha256:` digest. Neither service declares a `user:`, so both run as whatever uid their image defaults to. The service that terminates untrusted traffic and the service that holds the session signing key are both affected.
findings.impact: Today's deployment is not reproducibly the same as yesterday's, and a compromised or re-pushed tag reaches production without any change in this repository — on the two containers that see untrusted input and hold the signing key respectively.
findings.recommendation: Pin both by digest (`envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30.x@sha256:...`) and add an explicit non-root `user:` to each service.

triage.reason: No admission controller, image policy or signature verification appears anywhere in this repository; docker-compose.yml is the whole deployment definition given.
A registry-side immutable-tag policy or a Notary/cosign verification step could exist outside this repository; none is evidenced here, so UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. The severity is low either way.
There is no equivalent pinning elsewhere in the tree that would make this redundant.
